Every Bitcoin account comprises of two strings of characters. One is like your email address and it's called a "public key". Through the public key, you can receive Bitcoins from anyone in the world without risk of theft. The second string of characters is called a "private key" which corresponds to the public key (and is the equivalent of your email's password). Your Bitcoin wallet has the private and public keys paired and allows you to spend Bitcoins.

When you make a payment, just copy paste the merchant's public key into your Bitcoin wallet then the merchant will receive Bitcoins which does not compromise him in anyway, and your account isn't compromised because the private key isn't made public when you initiate a transaction.
Ok, but let's I get my hands on your keys. Are you just screwed?

If you get your hands on my private key, yes I'm screwed. Same way if you left cash lying somewhere in public you're screwed. If you want to protect your Bitcoins, private keys should be stored offline.

On the contrary, your questions are great (please feel free to ask more). It's much safer to pay in Bitcoin because the merchant has no need to store any keys (only his own). When you make a payment to the merchant's public key, he will see his account is receiving Bitcoins from someone's public key. Merchants (and anyone for that matter) can create multiple public keys per private key in order to keep track of who paid them. For example, a merchant can label a public key with my name and the product for his records and see when I paid (he can make sure it's me because he personally gave me the public key to pay him). The public ledger (aka the blockchain) verifies everyone's transactions through a network of task specific computers called miners and all you and I have to worry about is keeping our private keys safe.
